strengths: Clear identification and motivation of CSCNN's kernel incompleteness problem, with concrete examples (Example 3.2 for O(2,0))
Rigorous mathematical framework: Lemmas 4.1-4.2 properly derive equivariance constraints for conditional kernels; proofs are sound
Strong data efficiency results (Figure 3) convincingly demonstrate consistent advantages across multiple PDE tasks (NS, MW3, MW2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 15+ baselines, parameter-matched comparisons (except SWE-5), equivariance validation, and multiple diverse PDE tasks
Excellent presentation with clear structure and effective visualizations (Figures 1 and 3); well-motivated related work section
Practical contribution addressing recognized limitation of concurrent CSCNN work with low computational overhead
weaknesses: Main theoretical claim (Conjecture 4.1 on complete kernel basis) remains unproven despite being highlighted in title—only intuitive support for O(2,0) case via symbolic computation; no proof for general (p,q)

Mixed SOTA comparisons: SWE-5 results show CViT-L (92M params) significantly outperforms C-CSCNN Large (55M) with 1.56% vs 2.94% error, undermining scaling claims; fairness concerns from unmatched model sizes
Restrictive mean-field approximation via global mean pooling: loses spatial structure, represents significant expressivity trade-off, but insufficient analysis of alternatives or impact
Limited novelty in individual components: conditional kernels and mean pooling are established techniques; primary contribution is their combination for CSCNN-specific incompleteness
Incomplete treatment of non-linear operator properties: conditioning introduces non-linearity but implications for deep networks unexplored; relies on recent unfinished theory (Nyholm et al. 2025)
Missing practical analysis: no wall-clock time or memory comparisons; no ablation studies isolating component contributions; no discussion of when method helps most/least
Ad-hoc circular masking implementation (Appendix B.0.1) is critical for equivariance on discrete grids but lacks theoretical justification in main text

strengths: Clearly identifies and explains the incompleteness problem in CSCNN kernels with concrete mathematical examples (Example 3.2); excellent motivation
Provides rigorous equivariance proofs for the proposed conditional kernel framework (Lemmas 4.1-4.2, Proposition 4.1); theoretical contributions are sound where claims are made
Comprehensive experimental validation across 4 different PDE tasks with 14+ baselines and consistent improvements (33-54% over CSCNN); data efficiency experiments are particularly compelling
Honest acknowledgment that Conjecture 4.1 (completeness) is unproven and that mean pooling represents a trade-off between expressivity and efficiency
Well-organized presentation with clear problem setup; good use of illustrative examples and comprehensive appendices with implementation details
weaknesses: Central theoretical claim (Conjecture 4.1 on kernel basis completeness) is unproven—only symbolic computations for O(2,0) provided. Paper claims to address 'incomplete kernel basis' but main completeness proof is missing, undermining the core contribution. Misleading to state kernel basis is 'complete' when this is unproven.

Mean pooling as conditioning operator is a severe approximation: global averaging eliminates spatial structure entirely and it is unclear how much of theoretical completeness is actually recovered. No direct empirical validation that C-CSCNN kernels can represent previously-missing frequency components.

Insufficient ablation studies and expressivity analysis: no comparison of learned kernel properties, no visualization of frequency content, no comparison across different pooling operators (max, learnable, spatial), no sensitivity analysis. Unclear if improvements stem from completeness or from the conditioning mechanism itself.

Limited improvements on realistic scaling: SWE-5 results show C-CSCNN (55M) matches but does not exceed CViT-L (92M, 1.56% vs 2.94% error). Demonstrates competitive but not superior performance, undermining significance of contribution.

Experimental compromises: SWE-5 uses different model sizes (breaks parameter-matching protocol), no error bars/statistical significance tests, equivariance error slightly higher for C-CS (3.4e-7 vs 2.4e-7), hyperparameters sourced from other papers (reproducibility concerns)

Relatively incremental contribution: once incompleteness is identified, conditioning kernels on input is a straightforward solution. Mean pooling implementation is simple; limited novelty in the core mechanism itself.

Mean-field approximation not justified: why use crude global average rather than exploring spatial pooling, hierarchical methods, or learnable conditioning? Section 4.3 rushes through this critical design choice with little analysis.

strengths: Clear identification and explanation of the incompleteness limitation in CSCNNs, with concrete examples (Example 3.2) demonstrating how angular frequency components cannot propagate
Rigorous theoretical framework with correct proofs of equivariance constraints (Lemmas 4.1-4.2, Corollary 4.1, Proposition 4.1) showing conditional kernels maintain E(p,q)-equivariance
Thoughtful practical implementation strategy using mean pooling and circular masking to balance expressivity with computational efficiency while maintaining equivariance on discretized grids

Comprehensive experimental validation across four diverse PDE systems with data efficiency analysis, scaling studies, and equivariance verification demonstrating consistent 33-54% improvements over baseline CSCNNs

Strong empirical results particularly in low-data regimes, competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods (Transolver, CViT), and effective handling of relativistic physics where other baselines fail by construction
weaknesses: Central theoretical claim (Conjecture 4.1 on kernel basis completeness) remains unproven—only empirically validated; this is problematic for a paper claiming to address incompleteness, and the justification that proof would contradict implicit kernel philosophy is unsatisfying

Core methodological novelty is incremental: conditioning kernel networks on auxiliary inputs is relatively straightforward; primary contribution is applying existing equivariance theory to the conditional case rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts

Substantial theory-practice gap: theory permits conditioning on f(x) and f(y) but implementation restrictively uses only global mean pooling; acknowledged as 'less expressive' but alternatives are not explored or compared

Missing ablation studies on key design choices: no exploration of different conditioning operators T, no comparison of mean pooling alternatives (max pooling, learnable pooling), no analysis of circular mask radius sensitivity, and no timing benchmarks despite efficiency claims

Incomplete presentation with broken reference on page 9 ('Zhdanov et al., 20'); implementation details scattered across appendices reduces accessibility; missing mechanistic explanation of why mean pooling is effective for PDEs
Limited experimental scope: all tests on relatively small spatial grids (32³ to 192×96); scalability to larger domains common in practice is unclear
No comparative baseline for alternative incompleteness solutions (e.g., stacking additional CSCNN layers); limited discussion of computational cost trade-offs

strengths: Clear problem identification: Kernel basis incompleteness of CSCNNs is well-motivated and rigorously demonstrated through Example 3.6 (O(2,0) case), showing geometric product operations fail to propagate angular information beyond grade-1

Elegant theoretical solution: Conditioning kernels on input-derived multivectors naturally enables angular information propagation; simpler than original suggestion of doubling parameters through consecutive convolutions

Sound theoretical development: Lemma 4.2 correctly derives steerability constraints for conditional kernels; Lemmas 4.3 and Corollary 4.4 properly establish E(p,q)-equivariance preservation; Proposition 4.5 elegantly connects template matching to equivariance via operator T

Comprehensive experimental validation: Data efficiency analysis shows significant improvements with limited training data; equivariance empirically verified (~3.4×10⁻⁷ relative error); thorough ablation studies demonstrate importance of equivariant conditioning; comparison against 15 baselines across 4 diverse PDE tasks
Strong empirical improvements: Substantial gains over CSCNN baseline (33.9%-54.1% error reduction); competitive with state-of-the-art, achieving best performance on fluid dynamics tasks (NS, SWE-1)

Excellent reproducibility: Detailed implementation details in appendices, training specifications, dataset descriptions, and helper code provided; minimal computational overhead (0.87% slower than CSCNN)

Honest limitations discussion: Authors explicitly acknowledge unproven completeness conjecture for general O(p,q), task-dependent performance gains, and practical implementation workarounds; good faith treatment of limitations
weaknesses: Unproven completeness conjecture for general O(p,q): Main theoretical claim (Conjecture 4.7) rigorously proven only for O(2,0). Authors acknowledge the general proof is 'highly non-trivial' and leave it for future work. This significantly limits the theoretical contribution's generality, and empirical improvements across multiple symmetry groups, while suggestive, do not constitute proof

Task-dependent performance limitations: Strong improvements on fluid dynamics (53.7%-54.1% gains) but weaker on electrodynamics where Transolver remains superior. Authors suggest 'richer conditioning operators may be needed for non-local settings,' indicating the simple mean pooling conditioning may only partially address the underlying expressivity limitation

Limited exploration of conditioning operator sophistication: Despite theory allowing arbitrary conditioning, only mean pooling is thoroughly investigated. Acknowledgment that 'more complex...conditioning operators' are needed suggests the current solution may be incomplete. This raises questions about whether more expressive alternatives would substantially improve performance, particularly on non-local tasks

Theoretical-practical gap in implementation: Several design choices appear ad-hoc rather than theory-driven, including circular masking to maintain discrete equivariance (Section B.1, Figure 4) and grade-wise normalization required for MW2 stability. This suggests the theoretical framework doesn't fully capture discrete grid realization challenges
No code availability mentioned: Despite strong reproducibility details, absence of public code release limits broader impact and reproducibility verification for geometric deep learning community

Limited scaling analysis: Scaling properties examined only for SWE-5 task. Relative L² error gap to CViT-L widens at larger scales (1.56% vs 2.94%), suggesting potential scalability limitations not fully explored

Incomplete analysis of task-dependent failures: Substantial underperformance versus Transolver on non-local electromagnetic tasks (MW3, MW2) lacks detailed investigation. Root cause analysis of why simple conditioning fails for non-local dynamics would strengthen the contribution

strengths: Clear identification and explanation of CSCNN kernel basis incompleteness with concrete mathematical exposition (Example 3.6)
Mathematically sound derivation of equivariance constraints for conditional kernels (Lemmas 4.2-4.3, Corollary 4.4)
Practical solution balancing expressivity and efficiency through template matching with mean pooling
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 PDE tasks with 15 baselines, including data efficiency and scaling analyses
Honest discussion of limitations, including unproven completeness conjecture and limitations of simple conditioning operators
weaknesses: Central theoretical claim (Conjecture 4.7 on completeness for arbitrary O(p,q)) remains unproven; proof only provided for O(2,0) using symbolic computation, undermining theoretical contributions for general case

Mixed and task-dependent empirical results: method achieves only second-best on electrodynamics tasks (MW3, MW2 behind Transolver) and underperforms on SWE-5 scaling (CViT-L: 1.56% vs C-CSCNN: 2.94%); no systematic analysis of performance variations

Limited conceptual novelty: conditioning networks on input features is standard; the mechanism (equivariant MLP + conditioning) is straightforward; insight about geometric products propagating angular information is incremental

Over-simplified conditioning operator: only mean pooling tested, which is a mean-field approximation discarding spatial structure; authors acknowledge more complex problems need richer operators but don't explore this

Theory-practice gap: Lemma 4.2 derives constraint for conditioning on f(x) and f(y), but implementation uses only global T[f]; circular masking presented as ad-hoc fix for equivariance on discrete grids
Insufficient experimental analysis: no investigation of what conditioning learns, similar equivariance errors don't distinguish methods, limited ablations, no sensitivity analysis for hyperparameters
Presentation issues: key details scattered across appendices (circular masking, normalization), Conjecture 4.7 limitation downplayed, notation introduced without sufficient motivation
Reproducibility concerns: code release not mentioned, critical implementation details in appendices, hyperparameter choices lack principled justification

strengths: Well-motivated identification of kernel incompleteness in CSCNNs with concrete demonstration (Example 3.6) using symbolic computation and frequency analysis
Sound mathematical framework with correct derivation of G-steerability constraint for conditional kernels (Lemma 4.2) and proper equivariance analysis
Strong and consistent empirical results: 33.9%-54.1% error reduction over CSCNNs across diverse PDE tasks, with improvements consistent across different training set sizes (Figure 2)
Comprehensive experimental validation against 15+ strong baselines across multiple domains (fluid dynamics, relativistic electrodynamics) with proper equivariance verification
Excellent reproducibility: detailed implementation appendices, code snippets for verification, hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, and helpful ablation study (Table 3)
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging unproven conjecture for general O(p,q), discretization issues, and need for richer conditioning operators
weaknesses: Main theoretical claim (Conjecture 4.7 on kernel completeness for arbitrary O(p,q)) remains unproven—only O(2,0) formally verified. This fundamentally weakens the central theoretical contribution despite empirical evidence

Mean pooling approximation reduces to global mean-field, losing spatial structure and expressivity. Authors acknowledge it is 'less expressive' than full conditioning, but theoretical/empirical characterization of this loss is limited

Limited scalability: method advantages diminish at larger model sizes (Table 2, SWE-5). 55M parameter model underperforms CViT-L (92M) and trails state-of-the-art at scale, suggesting utility primarily in data-limited small-model regime
Discretization breaks exact equivariance on discrete grids (acknowledged). Circular masking workaround is pragmatic but ad-hoc; claimed negligible errors are not quantified

Incremental novelty over prior work: core implicit parameterization framework from Zhdanov et al. (2023, 2024); main contribution is conditioning on input, which while clever is relatively incremental

Performance not universally best: Transolver achieves substantially better results on MW2/MW3 (non-local electrodynamics tasks). Authors suggest richer conditioning operators needed but don't fully explore this
Dense notation and presentation may limit accessibility; intuitive explanation of why angular information fails to propagate in standard CSCNNs could be clearer
